paragraphs: Prediction sets express uncertainty by giving a collection of plausible outcomes instead of a single guess. This paper studies how to produce these sets as observations arrive over time, even when the process generating the data changes in unknown ways. The challenge is to keep their coverage frequency near a chosen target.

The proposed adaptive conformal inference method wraps around an existing predictor. That predictor can supply either a point prediction or estimated quantiles, so the approach does not require a particular prediction architecture. Its central move is to treat adaptation as learning one parameter whose best value changes over time and must be continually re-estimated.

The theoretical result concerns coverage across long time intervals: the method achieves the desired frequency regardless of the underlying data-generating process. This differs from guaranteeing coverage separately at every moment. Unlike earlier conformal approaches described in the abstract, it does not rely on exchangeability. Tests on two real-world datasets also show robustness to substantial, visible distribution changes.
neurips-2021-adaptive-conformal-inferenc.tldr: Adaptive conformal inference continually adjusts prediction sets to achieve target coverage over long intervals despite unknown distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Medical image translation faces a training-data tradeoff. Supervised Pix2Pix can perform well but needs paired images with precise pixel alignment. Motion or anatomical changes can make that requirement difficult to satisfy. Cycle-consistency methods accept unpaired or misaligned images, but the abstract describes their translation performance as potentially less satisfactory.

RegGAN addresses this tradeoff by treating target-image misalignment as noise in the training labels. Alongside the image generator, it trains a registration network that adaptively accounts for that misalignment. Drawing on loss-correction theory, the approach seeks a shared solution to translation and registration, allowing the training objective to account for spatial disagreement between images.

The authors incorporate RegGAN into several existing translation methods and report improved performance. In their results, it exceeds Pix2Pix on aligned data and cycle-consistency approaches on misaligned or unpaired data. A CycleGAN using RegGAN also surpasses NICEGAN with fewer network parameters. These findings support jointly addressing alignment and translation when precisely aligned medical training images are difficult to obtain.
neurips-2021-breaking-the-dilemma-of-med.tldr: RegGAN jointly learns image translation and registration by treating misalignment as label noise, improving results across the reported medical imaging settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies the unavoidable computational difficulty of a particular class of min-max problems. One variable is chosen to minimize an objective while another is chosen to maximize it. The objective is smooth, nonconvex in the minimizing variable, and strongly concave in the maximizing variable. The target is an approximately stationary point.

The authors establish lower bounds on calls to a first-order oracle, which supplies information used by gradient-based methods. For deterministic oracles, the bound scales as sqrt(kappa) times epsilon^(-2), where epsilon specifies the stationarity tolerance and kappa is the condition number. Its dependence on both quantities matches the best existing upper bound apart from logarithmic factors.

For stochastic oracles, the lower bound becomes sqrt(kappa) times epsilon^(-2) plus kappa^(1/3) times epsilon^(-4). The cited upper bound instead scales as kappa^3 times epsilon^(-4). Thus, the deterministic result closely pins down the required complexity, while the stochastic result leaves a gap in condition-number dependence. That gap identifies unresolved theoretical room between known algorithmic guarantees and established lower limits.
neurips-2021-complexity-lower-bounds-for.tldr: The paper establishes near-matching deterministic complexity lower bounds for nonconvex–strongly-concave min-max optimization and a remaining gap for stochastic methods.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether training a neural network can approach the best prediction quality permitted by the underlying data distribution. It studies shallow ReLU networks trained by gradient descent with logistic loss for binary classification. The setting allows general data distributions, including those where even an optimal classifier makes some errors.

The main result shows that early-stopped training can bring population performance arbitrarily close to optimal for both logistic loss and misclassification loss. It also establishes a probability-estimation result: applying a sigmoid to the network output can approximate the true conditional label probabilities arbitrarily finely. The guarantee therefore addresses both classification and the reliability of probabilistic predictions.

The analysis connects the required training iterations, sample size, and network architecture to a complexity measure of the true conditional model. It also shows that classifiers satisfying a specified local interpolation property are inconsistent. This provides a reason to examine how training fits individual observations, but it does not establish that early stopping is necessary; the abstract explicitly distinguishes that stronger claim from the result proved.
neurips-2021-early-stopped-neural-networ.tldr: Early-stopped gradient descent on shallow ReLU networks can approach optimal classification and probability estimation, even when labels are inherently uncertain.

paragraphs: In truncated linear regression, an observation becomes visible only when its outcome falls within a specified set. Otherwise, both the outcome and its accompanying features are hidden, including the fact that the pair exists. The observed data therefore represent a selected portion of the underlying regression problem, making parameter estimation more difficult.

Earlier efficient estimators described in the abstract handled normally distributed errors with known variance. This paper extends the estimation problem to unknown noise variance, estimating both the regression coefficients and the amount of noise. The authors present their method as the first estimator for this setting that is efficient in both computation and statistical use of data.

The method uses projected stochastic gradient descent to optimize the negative log-likelihood of the truncated observations. Accounting for truncation in that objective is central to learning from the selected sample. The authors also establish asymptotic normality of estimation errors and use it to construct explicit confidence regions. The contribution thus includes uncertainty quantification alongside efficient estimation of the model and noise variance.
neurips-2021-efficient-truncated-linear-.tldr: The paper efficiently estimates regression coefficients and unknown noise variance from truncated observations, with asymptotic results supporting explicit confidence regions.

paragraphs: Weak supervision combines imperfect labeling sources to reduce the need for manually collected ground-truth labels. The paper examines approaches that train without labeled training data. In the existing workflow described by the authors, one model first combines the weak sources into probabilistic labels, and a separate downstream model then learns from those labels.

This separation creates two difficulties: the label model relies on assumptions that may not hold in practice, and its learning objective does not account for downstream predictive performance. The proposed approach connects the stages through end-to-end learning. It uses a neural network to reparameterize earlier probabilistic posteriors and trains the downstream predictor to agree with the resulting probabilistic labels.

The reported results show better downstream test performance than prior work and greater robustness when weak labeling sources depend on one another. Such dependencies matter because several sources can provide overlapping information rather than independent evidence. The findings support learning the probabilistic supervision and final predictor together, with the usefulness of the supervision tied more directly to the model that ultimately makes predictions.
neurips-2021-end-to-end-weak-supervision.tldr: An end-to-end weak-supervision approach jointly connects probabilistic labeling with downstream learning, improving reported accuracy and robustness to dependent labeling sources.

paragraphs: Keyword search on a graph seeks a subtree or subgraph containing the requested keywords, with results ordered by a chosen criterion. The paper focuses on graphs where some edges or keywords are missing. In that setting, relevant information can be obscured by incomplete connections or descriptions, undermining methods that assume the graph is complete.

KS-GNN combines a graph neural network with an autoencoder to learn compact representations of nodes. These representations preserve information about both graph structure and keyword features. The model also considers latent relationships and how frequently different keywords occur, aiming to reduce the damage caused by missing information when representing and searching the graph.

The authors report that their model answers keyword queries over incomplete graphs with linear time complexity. Experiments on four real-world datasets show consistently better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods when information is missing. The contribution is therefore both representational and computational: it learns node descriptions suited to incomplete data while supporting efficient query answering, with empirical gains demonstrated in the tested graphs.
neurips-2021-ks-gnn-keywords-search-over.tldr: KS-GNN learns structural and keyword representations that improve keyword search on incomplete graphs while supporting linear-time query answering.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for robotics often needs substantial interaction data. Planning can use an available model to reduce that demand, but its performance suffers when the model inaccurately describes the robot or its surroundings. This paper starts from the observation that these approaches have complementary strengths: learning can adapt behavior, while planning supplies useful structure from approximate knowledge.

Learning to Execute, or L2E, combines them by training universal policies conditioned on plans. An approximate plan becomes information supplied to the learned policy, connecting model-based guidance with learned execution. The central idea is to make use of what the plan contains even when the model that produced it is imprecise or wrong.

In robotic manipulation experiments, L2E performs better than pure reinforcement learning, pure planning, and the compared methods that combine learning with planning. These results support plan conditioning as a useful way to integrate the two approaches. The reported contribution is a framework for learning how to execute with approximate guidance, with its performance advantage demonstrated in the manipulation experiments.
neurips-2021-learning-to-execute-efficie.tldr: Learning to Execute trains policies conditioned on approximate plans, outperforming the tested planning, reinforcement-learning, and hybrid alternatives in robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: Large pretrained Transformers can be difficult to deploy under tight latency constraints. NxM sparsity offers a hardware-supported way to reduce their parameters: within each contiguous group of N parameters, M can be retained at arbitrary positions. The challenge is to impose that pattern while preserving downstream performance, especially when fine-tuning data are limited.

NxMTransformer formulates sparsification as constrained optimization. It uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM, to separate the task into two subproblems solved sequentially. This connects the downstream learning objective with the required hardware-compatible sparsity pattern, producing Transformer models that retain high accuracy and can execute effectively on hardware supporting that pattern.

Across the evaluated language tasks, the authors report a GLUE score 1.7 points above current best practices. They also analyze how ADMM affects fine-tuning accuracy and show further performance improvement when combining the approach with knowledge distillation. The findings support treating sparsity as an explicit training constraint, with predictive quality and hardware requirements addressed within the same optimization framework.
neurips-2021-nxmtransformer-semi-structu.tldr: NxMTransformer uses ADMM to impose hardware-compatible sparsity on pretrained language models, improving reported GLUE performance over existing sparsification practices.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit repeatedly chooses among actions while learning their average rewards. Because later choices depend on earlier outcomes, the collected observations are adaptive rather than independent and identically distributed. The paper argues that ordinary sample averages can then have bias and unfavorable statistical properties, leaving room for better inference within otherwise effective decision algorithms.

The proposed doubly adaptive Thompson sampling algorithm, DATS, draws on causal-inference methods. It adaptively reweights the terms of a doubly robust estimator for each action's mean reward while retaining the exploration behavior of Thompson sampling. This changes how accumulated evidence is interpreted, aiming to improve decisions made from adaptively collected observations.

Across 20 synthetic domains and a semi-synthetic experiment based on a web-service A/B test, DATS achieves better empirical regret and best-arm identification sample complexity than the compared UCB and Thompson sampling methods. A finite-time regret bound also matches their bounds up to logarithmic factors. The results therefore combine practical improvements in the tested settings with a worst-case guarantee of comparable order.
neurips-2021-online-multi-armed-bandits-.tldr: Doubly adaptive Thompson sampling improves inference from adaptive bandit data, yielding empirical gains while retaining comparable worst-case regret guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how neural-network design can encode useful assumptions about uncertainty. Its focus is Bayesian neural networks, where a prior over weights induces a prior over possible functions. The authors seek function-space biases that help models recognize unfamiliar inputs, addressing the broader concern that networks can reinforce hidden biases in their training data.

The theoretical contribution connects periodic activation functions with translation-invariant, stationary Gaussian process priors. Stationarity means that the prior's relationships between inputs are unchanged by a common translation. The connection links the choice of weight prior to that function-space behavior. It applies beyond sinusoidal activations, also covering triangular waves and periodic versions of ReLU.

Experiments show comparable performance on in-domain data and sensitivity to perturbed inputs that supports out-of-domain detection in deep networks. These findings suggest that periodic activations can influence uncertainty-related behavior while maintaining predictive performance on familiar data. The paper's contribution is the theoretical link between architectural choices and stationary priors, together with empirical evidence of useful responses to unfamiliar inputs.
neurips-2021-periodic-activation-functio.tldr: Periodic activations connect Bayesian neural networks to stationary Gaussian process priors and show useful sensitivity to out-of-domain inputs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can fail to distinguish graph structures that matter for a task. More expressive alternatives may be harder to implement or scale, and increased theoretical power does not automatically yield better real-world performance. This paper investigates graph reconstruction—recovering information about a graph from its subgraphs—as a way to address these connected challenges.

The authors use reconstruction to build two classes of expressive graph representations. They also show how reconstruction can increase the expressive power of any GNN architecture. Beyond distinguishing structures, the approach supplies a provably powerful inductive bias for invariance to vertex removal, linking the representation strategy to how a model handles changes in graph membership.

Empirically, reconstruction enables solutions to seven graph-property tasks that the original GNN cannot solve, while preserving invariance to permutations of vertex labels. It also improves state-of-the-art GNN performance across nine real-world benchmark datasets. These findings connect formal expressiveness with practical prediction gains, showing that information extracted through subgraphs can strengthen existing GNNs in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2021-reconstruction-for-powerful.tldr: Graph reconstruction strengthens GNN expressiveness while preserving vertex-permutation invariance and improves performance on the reported synthetic and real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasts help decision makers estimate the losses associated with possible actions before using them. Ordinary calibration asks whether predicted probabilities agree with observed frequencies on average. This paper shows that such average agreement can still be insufficient for accurately predicting losses in regression problems where decisions depend on an outcome crossing a cutoff.

The authors introduce threshold calibration, a stronger requirement tailored to these decisions. They characterize it as exactly the condition needed for accurate loss prediction for threshold decisions. They also provide an efficient algorithm that accepts an uncalibrated forecaster and provably produces a threshold-calibrated one, allowing downstream users to estimate losses across threshold decisions and threshold loss functions.

The distinction matters because a forecast can look reliable in aggregate yet give misleading estimates for the particular cutoff a decision maker uses. In hospital scheduling and resource allocation experiments, threshold calibration improves decision-loss prediction without reducing decision quality. The result concerns making the anticipated consequences of threshold-based actions more trustworthy, with empirical support in those two application settings.
neurips-2021-reliable-decisions-with-thr.tldr: Threshold calibration gives the precise calibration condition needed to predict threshold-decision losses accurately and improves such predictions in two real-world settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may generalize better when training environments provide appropriate diversity and difficulty. This paper examines how selecting previously generated levels can participate in environment design. It reframes Prioritized Level Replay, or PLR, which selectively revisits random training levels, as a form of unsupervised environment design that adapts training experiences to the agent.

The authors introduce Dual Curriculum Design, a framework containing both PLR and PAIRED as special cases. This connection brings theoretical tools from environment design to replay and yields a PLR version with a robustness guarantee at Nash equilibria. The guarantee is tied to that equilibrium condition, giving a theoretical basis for a method previously motivated mainly by empirical success.

The theory also motivates a counterintuitive change: prevent policy updates on uncurated levels and train through the selected replay curriculum. The resulting PLR-perpendicular method can improve convergence to Nash equilibria despite using less data for updates. Experiments report better out-of-distribution zero-shot transfer results and improved PAIRED performance, supporting selective training as a useful part of environment design.
neurips-2021-replay-guided-adversarial-e.tldr: A unified theory of replay and environment design motivates selective policy updates that improve reported transfer performance and provide equilibrium-based robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Distributed training often exchanges gradients instead of raw examples, but those updates can still reveal sensitive information. This paper focuses on recovering the labels associated with training samples. Earlier approaches described in the abstract either extracted labels analytically for certain models or reconstructed labels and inputs together using additional knowledge about the model's current state.

The proposed method discovers the set of training labels using only the gradient of the final layer and the mapping from label identifiers to labels. The authors describe it as applicable across a wide variety of model architectures and domains. Its input requirements clarify the exposure being studied: information in the transmitted update can reveal label membership without transmitting the original examples.

Experiments demonstrate the method in image classification and automatic speech recognition. Combining it with existing reconstruction techniques also improves their effectiveness. On the defensive side, the authors show that gradient quantization and sparsification can substantially reduce attack success. These results identify both a source of label leakage and tested ways to reduce it, without claiming that those transformations eliminate leakage altogether.
neurips-2021-revealing-and-protecting-la.tldr: Final-layer gradients can reveal training-label sets, while quantization and sparsification substantially reduce the demonstrated attack's success.

paragraphs: A GAN can produce convincing samples overall while representing less common parts of the data poorly. The paper focuses on low-density regions, including minor groups, where generated samples often have lower quality. It seeks to improve their representation without the loss of diversity that can accompany techniques modifying the data distribution or filtering generated outputs.

The proposed method diagnoses underrepresentation during training using statistics of the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution at individual data instances. The authors observe that poorly represented samples can have either a large average discrepancy or a discrepancy that varies substantially. They use these signals to give such samples greater emphasis during GAN training.

Experiments across several datasets show improved GAN performance, with particularly strong benefits for the quality and diversity of samples from minor groups. The approach matters because it uses information about the model's own changing mismatch with the data to guide training attention. Its reported results support addressing uneven representation directly during learning, alongside the broader goal of maintaining overall sample quality.
neurips-2021-self-diagnosing-gan-diagnos.tldr: A GAN training method identifies underrepresented examples through discrepancy statistics and improves reported sample quality and diversity, especially for minor groups.

paragraphs: Shift invariance helps an image classifier treat shifted versions of an image consistently. This paper investigates a possible cost of that useful property: invariance to circular shifts can increase sensitivity to adversarial perturbations. The argument combines analysis of simplified classifiers with experiments using realistic architectures and real datasets.

For shift-invariant linear classifiers, the authors show that the margin between classes can depend only on the signal's DC component, its constant or average component. They then use results about infinitely wide networks to identify simple cases where fully connected and shift-invariant neural networks have linear decision boundaries. This connects the linear analysis to particular neural-network settings.

The authors prove the existence of adversarial examples in a two-class construction involving a black or white dot on a gray background. They also report reduced adversarial robustness from shift invariance in their real-data experiments and investigate the connection further with synthetic data. Together, these results show that a useful invariance can carry a robustness cost; the theoretical constructions and empirical findings do not assert that every shift-invariant model must behave identically.
neurips-2021-shift-invariance-can-reduce.tldr: Theoretical examples and empirical tests show that circular-shift invariance can make classifiers more vulnerable to adversarial perturbations.

paragraphs: Public goods games model situations where individual contributions are costly but benefit others. This paper takes the viewpoint of a central planner overseeing a network of self-interested agents in a best-shot game. The planner seeks equilibria that optimize a desired criterion, addressing shortcomings of existing methods that return suboptimal solutions and focus only on social welfare.

The method uses a correspondence between game equilibria and maximal independent sets in graphs. It defines a Markov decision process that builds such a set incrementally, then uses planning to search for equilibria. A graph neural network policy subsequently learns from demonstrations of that search, turning the planner's decisions into a faster procedure for unseen game instances.

The planning method outperforms existing approaches in the evaluation. On the largest tested graphs, the learned policy reaches 99.5% of the planner's performance while being three orders of magnitude faster to evaluate. This shows a strong empirical tradeoff between solution quality and evaluation speed. The authors also identify potential applicability to broader public goods games and other graph combinatorial optimization problems.
neurips-2021-solving-graph-based-public-.tldr: Tree search finds strong public-goods equilibria, and an imitation-trained graph policy nearly matches its performance with much faster evaluation on the largest tested graphs.

paragraphs: For highly imbalanced classification, the paper identifies area under the precision-recall curve, or AUPRC, as a more appropriate evaluation measure than area under the ROC curve. Yet principled stochastic methods for directly optimizing AUPRC have received less attention. The authors develop a deep-learning training approach centered on this evaluation objective.

Their approach maximizes average precision, which the abstract describes as an unbiased point estimator of AUPRC. They express the objective as a sum of dependent compositional functions: inner computations depend on random variables also involved at the outer level. This dependence is central to the optimization problem, motivating algorithms designed around its structure.

The resulting SOAP family includes adaptive and non-adaptive stochastic algorithms with provable convergence under mild conditions. Experiments on image and graph datasets show better AUPRC than prior methods on the evaluated imbalanced problems. The contribution combines a training objective aligned with the chosen metric, algorithms that handle its nested dependencies, and conditional convergence guarantees, with an implementation made available in the libAUC library.
neurips-2021-stochastic-optimization-of-.tldr: SOAP optimizes average precision with stochastic algorithms that have conditional convergence guarantees and improve reported AUPRC on imbalanced image and graph tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents can reason about extended courses of action through options, which support predictions over longer time scales than individual actions. This paper asks how those predictions should reflect the fact that a course of action may be relevant or feasible only in certain situations. It formalizes that idea through affordances for options.

The authors develop partial option models that account for where an option is affordable. Such models restrict their scope according to the situations in which the option is appropriate. The analysis examines how this choice affects estimation and approximation errors during learning and planning, making explicit the tradeoff involved in using a model with a deliberately limited scope.

The paper also demonstrates learning both affordances and partial option models online. In the Taxi domain, this improves sample efficiency and planning time. These results suggest that learning where an extended action is relevant can make its predictive model more useful computationally and statistically. The evidence combines a formal treatment of the error tradeoffs with an empirical demonstration in that domain.
neurips-2021-temporally-abstract-partial.tldr: Partial option models learn where extended actions are feasible or relevant, improving sample efficiency and planning time in the Taxi domain.

paragraphs: An agent's decisions can have very different consequences depending on whether their effects can be undone. This paper develops a way for reinforcement-learning agents to estimate that distinction from experience. Its theoretical starting point is that approximate reversibility can be learned through a surrogate task: determining the chronological order of randomly sampled trajectory events.

The intuition is that events consistently observed in the same order are likely to be separated by an irreversible sequence of actions. Temporal ordering supplies its own training information, so the reversibility estimate can be learned without prior knowledge. The authors incorporate this estimate into two strategies, one guiding exploration and another guiding control.

Experiments demonstrate the potential of these strategies in several environments, including Sokoban. In synthetic tasks, the authors learn control policies that never fail and produce no interaction side effects, even without access to the reward function. Those outcomes are specific to the reported tasks. More broadly, the work shows how a self-supervised temporal signal can inform decisions about actions whose consequences may be difficult to reverse.
neurips-2021-there-is-no-turning-back-a-.tldr: Learning the temporal order of experienced events provides a self-supervised signal for reversibility that can guide exploration and control.

paragraphs: Driving simulators can generate abundant labeled data, but perception models trained on those images and sensor readings still face a gap when used on real data. This paper studies how to use simulation more effectively, focusing primarily on training with labels from the synthetic domain alone. Its perspective comes from domain-adaptation theory.

The approach addresses both what the network learns and which simulated examples it sees. It introduces a principled method for learning invariant representations and a theoretically motivated view of sampling simulator data. The framework is described as independent of a particular network architecture or simulator, making those training choices applicable across different implementations.

The authors demonstrate the framework on bird's-eye-view vehicle segmentation using camera and lidar data from CARLA, then evaluate it on nuScenes. They also examine variations in weather, asset counts, map design, and color diversity, identifying which matter to trained perception networks and which their adaptation technique can compensate for. This connects simulator content choices with representation learning as two parts of addressing the reality gap.
neurips-2021-towards-optimal-strategies-.tldr: The paper combines invariant representation learning with principled simulator sampling to address transfer from synthetic driving data to real-world perception.

paragraphs: Training a separate graph neural network for every large graph can be expensive. This paper investigates how pretraining can produce representations that transfer between graphs, with theoretical guidance for both the learning objective and the conditions supporting transfer. It proposes capturing essential graph information as the goal of transferable GNN training.

That perspective motivates Ego-Graph Information maximization, or EGI. The method is designed to capture the proposed information analytically. Under the assumption that node features are relevant to graph structure, the authors analyze transferability through differences between local graph Laplacians in source and target graphs. This links transfer behavior to a concrete comparison of local structural information.

Controlled synthetic experiments support the theoretical conclusions. Experiments on two real-world network datasets produce consistent results for direct transfer, the setting covered by the analysis. Additional experiments on large knowledge graphs show promising outcomes when transfer includes fine-tuning. The paper therefore distinguishes its analyzed setting from the broader practical setting, combining conditional theoretical insight with evidence for both forms of reuse.
neurips-2021-transfer-learning-of-graph-.tldr: EGI learns transferable graph representations and relates transferability to local structural differences when node features carry structural information.

paragraphs: This paper studies elections between two alternatives when preferences depend on an unobserved state. Each voter receives a private signal correlated with that state. The model includes voters who always favor one alternative as well as voters whose preference changes with the state, so the election must aggregate both information and differing preferences.

Simply having voters act on their own signals can fail even when everyone has state-dependent preferences. If those signals are systematically biased, the resulting vote need not select the alternative that everyone would prefer. The problem is therefore not just counting expressed choices: the mechanism must account for the relationship between private information and the underlying state.

The authors present a mechanism that elicits and aggregates signals to select the alternative favored by the majority. Within their model, truthful reporting forms a strong Bayes Nash equilibrium, meaning no coalition can deviate to obtain a better outcome. This combines an information-aggregation objective with an incentive guarantee, addressing whether voters have reason to provide the information the mechanism needs.
neurips-2021-wisdom-of-the-crowd-voting-.tldr: A two-alternative voting mechanism aggregates private signals to select the majority-favored outcome while making truthful reporting a strong Bayes Nash equilibrium.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis motivates using a sparse subnetwork that can retain a full model's performance while reducing training and inference costs. Finding the sparse mask can itself be very expensive, making a discovered winning ticket valuable. This paper studies how its creator can embed evidence of ownership in that sparse structure.

The proposed lottery verification approach develops graph-based signatures that use the subnetwork's topology as credentials. This adds a structural route to ownership verification alongside approaches based on weights or predictions. Combining these signatures with trigger-set methods allows verification in both white-box and black-box settings, covering different levels of access to the model being checked.

Experiments use ResNet-20, ResNet-18, and ResNet-50 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The authors report effective verification and robustness to tested removal attacks, including fine-tuning and pruning, as well as several ambiguity attacks. These findings support sparse topology as a useful place to encode ownership evidence, with the demonstrated robustness tied to the models and attacks evaluated.
neurips-2021-you-are-caught-stealing-my-.tldr: Graph-based signatures embedded in winning-ticket topology enable ownership verification and withstand several tested removal and ambiguity attacks.
